p2.key: The single bond is one σ bond; the double bond is one σ and one π bond.

The π electrons are delocalized over both O–O bonds (two resonance structures; ozone is a resonance hybrid), so both bonds are identical (bond order 1.5). Their length is intermediate between the O–O single bond in H2O2 (longer) and the O=O double bond in O2 (shorter).
A curve of similar shape lying above (to the left of) the water curve, i.e. higher vapour pressure at every temperature – weaker intermolecular forces mean molecules escape more easily.
London (dispersion) forces – van der Waals' forces from temporary/induced dipoles between the layers.

Any two use + explanation pairs:

  • Pencil 'lead': weak forces between layers mean layers flake off onto paper.
  • Electrodes/conductor: each C uses 3 electrons in bonding, leaving delocalized (mobile) electrons that move along the layers.
  • Carbon fibres/strengthening: very strong covalent bonding within the extensive layers.

'Layers slide over each other' alone does not score for the pencil use.

(i) C: sp (two electron domains, linear); O: sp2 (three domains: one bond + two lone pairs).

(ii) After hybridization: three sp2 orbitals (lower) containing 2, 2 and 1 electrons, and one unhybridized 2p orbital at higher energy containing 1 electron (used for the π bond).

(iii) The ability of an atom to attract a shared (bonding) pair of electrons.

(iv) Across the period O has more protons (higher nuclear charge) with the same number of shells, and a smaller radius, so the bonding electrons are attracted more strongly.

Any two: O2 is non-polar; it cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so dissolving would require breaking strong H-bonds between water molecules; it can only form weak London (dispersion) forces with water, which do not compensate.
Hydrogen bonding. The O–H groups of the carboxylic acid hydrogen-bond to O atoms of neighbouring molecules; this is stronger than dipole–dipole or London forces.

H–O–C(=O)–C(=O)–O–H with all bonds as shared pairs: each C has one C=O double bond, one C–O single bond and the C–C bond. Each carbonyl O carries two lone pairs and each hydroxyl O carries two lone pairs. The mark is lost if any oxygen lone pairs are missing. Dots, crosses or lines are all accepted.

Acid: each COOH has one C=O (shorter) and one C–O (longer) bond, so the C–O bond lengths are different.

Conjugate base: in each COO⁻ group both C–O bonds are the same length, intermediate between single and double (bond order 1.5).

Why: the negative charge and π electrons are delocalized over both O atoms (resonance structures).

Name any three allotropes (1 mark) and describe each structure (3 marks):

  • Diamond: each C bonded tetrahedrally to 4 others (sp³) in a 3D covalent network
  • Graphite: each C bonded to 3 others (sp², trigonal planar) in hexagonal layers held by weak London forces
  • Fullerene (C₆₀): each C bonded to 3 others, forming a cage or sphere of hexagons and pentagons
  • Graphene: a single 2D layer of hexagonally arranged C atoms, each bonded to 3 others

σ bond: head-on (end-on, axial) overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis.

π bond: sideways overlap of p orbitals, with electron density above and below the axis. A C=C bond has one σ and one π bond.

SCl₂: bent (V-shaped), <109.5° (about 103°; 100–108° accepted), polar. There are 4 electron domains on S, 2 of them lone pairs.

SClF₅: octahedral, 90°, polar. There are 6 bonding domains, but one Cl replaces an F, so the dipoles do not cancel.

All six correct for [3]; 4–5 for [2]; 2–3 for [1].

(i) PBr₃: P has three P–Br bonds and one lone pair; each Br has three lone pairs. SF₄: S has four S–F bonds and one lone pair (expanded octet); each F has three lone pairs. Missing halogen lone pairs are penalized once.

(ii) PBr₃: 4 electron domains (1 lone pair), so the shape is trigonal pyramidal. Br–P–Br is about 100–108° (literature 101°), less than 109.5°.
SF₄: 5 electron domains (1 lone pair, which sits equatorial), so the shape is see-saw. Give any two angles: Fax–S–Fax ≈ 180° (about 173° actual), Feq–S–Feq <120° (about 102°), Fax–S–Feq ≈ 90°.

(iii) P–Br and S–F bonds are polar. Both shapes are asymmetric because of the lone pair, so the bond dipoles do not cancel and there is a net dipole.

(i) Either: a shared electron pair attracted electrostatically to both nuclei, formed by sharing electrons. Or: a σ bond formed by overlap of the H 1s orbital with an sp² orbital of C.

(ii) α (the O–H oxygen, 4 domains): sp³. β (the C=O oxygen, 3 domains): sp².

(iii) σ: head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals. π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals.

(iv) 11 σ and 3 π. The σ bonds are 2 C–H, 2 O–H, 2 C–O, 2 C–C, plus one σ in each of the C=C and 2 C=O. The π bonds are in the C=C and 2 C=O.

Compound C (butan-2-ol) has stronger intermolecular forces than but-2-ene, so but-2-ene is more volatile. Any two:

  • C forms hydrogen bonds (O–H)
  • C is more polar, with dipole–dipole forces
  • C has a greater molar mass, so stronger London forces

'Stronger IMF' alone scores [1].

(i) NF₄⁺: sp³ (4 bonding domains). N₂H₂: sp² (N=N double bond, 3 domains). N₂H₄: sp³ (3 bonds plus 1 lone pair).

(ii) σ: head-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis. π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, above and below the axis.

(iii) SF₄: four S–F bonds and one lone pair on S; each F has 3 lone pairs. The shape is see-saw.
SF₆: six S–F bonds with no lone pair on S; each F has 3 lone pairs. The shape is octahedral.

(i) CH₃CH₂CH₃ < CH₃CHO < CH₃CH₂OH < CH₃COOH

(ii)

  • propane: London forces only
  • ethanal: dipole–dipole forces (plus London)
  • ethanol and ethanoic acid: hydrogen bonding (plus dipole–dipole and London)
  • strength order: H-bonding > dipole–dipole > London
  • ethanoic acid forms more and stronger H-bonds (it can dimerize) and has more electrons than ethanol

(i) P in the centre bonded to three H atoms (three shared pairs) plus one lone pair on P.

(ii) sp3 (four electron domains: 3 bonding + 1 lone pair).

(iii) Lewis base – P has a lone pair it can donate.

(iv) Non-polar – P and H have the same (or very similar) electronegativity (2.2).

(v) PH3 has only London (dispersion) forces (weak dipole–dipole at most); NH3 forms hydrogen bonds, which are much stronger, so more energy is needed to separate NH3 molecules. Do not imply covalent bonds break.

(vi) Weak: only partially ionized/dissociated in solution (reversible equilibrium). Brønsted–Lowry base: a proton (H+) acceptor.

(i) Each structure has σ bonds N–N and N–O plus a π bond N–N; the remaining π electrons are delocalized over N–N–O (one structure has a second N≡N π bond, the other a N=O π bond).

(ii) Resonance: more than one valid Lewis structure can be drawn, differing only in the position of multiple (π) bonds/electrons; the real structure is a hybrid with fractional bond orders.

Ethane-1,2-diol has O–H groups, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules (ethene has only London forces); it also has stronger London forces (larger molecule). Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than other intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules. Do not suggest covalent bonds break.

C–C single bond joining two COO groups; each C has one C=O and one C–O−; every O carries its lone pairs (two on C=O oxygens, three on O−), with the 2− charge shown. Dots, crosses or lines are all accepted; do not draw resonance forms.

The π electrons are delocalized over each O–C–O group (resonance), so every C–O bond is identical, with a bond order of 1.5.

Length is between C–O (143 pm) and C=O (122 pm): about 130 pm (any value 123–142 pm).

(i) σ: head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals (s–s, s–p or p–p), with electron density on the internuclear axis. π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, with electron density above and below the axis.

(ii) Propane: 10 σ, 0 π. Propene: 8 σ, 1 π (the C=C is one σ + one π).

(i) Ionic – electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged K+ and Cl− ions.

(ii) TiCl4 has a simple molecular (covalent) structure; melting only overcomes the weak intermolecular forces (London forces) between molecules, not ionic bonds. Do not say that covalent bonds break.
About 107°: there are 4 electron domains around N, and the lone pair repels the bonds more strongly than bond pairs do, so the angle is less than 109.5°.
Electron domain geometry: tetrahedral (3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair). Hybridization: sp3.

Any two of:

  • the molecule is planar (X-ray evidence);
  • all C–C bond lengths are equal, intermediate between C–C and C=C;
  • all C–C–C bond angles are equal (120°).

Lewis structure: P bonded to three Cl atoms, with one lone pair on P and three lone pairs on each Cl.

Molecular geometry: trigonal pyramidal.

Bond angles: < 109.5° (about 100–107°), because the lone pair repels the bond pairs more strongly.

(i) N2 has a triple bond, while hydrazine has an N–N single bond. The triple bond is much stronger (945 vs 158 kJ mol−1) because more shared electron pairs attract both nuclei more strongly.

(ii) Hydrazine forms hydrogen bonds between its molecules (N–H groups); N2O4 cannot.

(iii) N2H4: −2. N2O4: +4.

(iv) N2H4 is the reducing agent: its N oxidation state increases (−2 → 0), so it is oxidized.

(i) A lone pair in a p orbital of the singly bonded O overlaps with the π electrons of the double bond, so the π electrons are delocalized over all three atoms. As a result, both O–O bonds have equal length (bond order 1.5, between O–O and O=O) and equal bond energy.

(ii) Structure O=O+–O−: the central O has a lone pair (one double bond, one single bond); the terminal O=O has 2 lone pairs and the terminal O–O has 3. Formal charges: 0 (double-bonded O), +1 (central O), −1 (single-bonded O).

PF3: P with three P–F single bonds and one lone pair; each F has three lone pairs. 4 electron domains, 3 bonding → trigonal pyramidal, bond angle <109.5° (≈107°; ~97° actual).

PF5: P with five P–F single bonds, no lone pair (expanded octet); each F has three lone pairs. 5 bonding domains → trigonal bipyramidal, bond angles 90° and 120° (and 180°).

Lone pairs on F must be shown for the Lewis marks.
PF3 is polar (pyramidal: bond dipoles do not cancel) and PF5 is non-polar (symmetrical trigonal bipyramid: bond dipoles cancel).
sp3 – P has four electron domains (three bonds + one lone pair).

Nitrogen: 4 electron domains (3 bonds + 1 lone pair) → electron domain geometry tetrahedral; molecular geometry trigonal pyramidal.

Carbon: 3 electron domains (C=O counts as one) → electron domain geometry trigonal planar; molecular geometry trigonal planar.

(i) Any one: urea has a greater molar mass/more electrons (stronger London forces); urea forms more hydrogen bonds per molecule; urea is more polar (greater dipole moment). Stronger intermolecular forces → solid.

(ii) Two sketches, each with a dashed line for the hydrogen bond in a straight line:
• H3N: ····H–O–H (lone pair on N attracts an H of water)
• H2O: ····H–NH2 (lone pair on O attracts an H of ammonia)
Show the lone pair on the N or O involved.
The lone pair on each N can be delocalized into the C–N bond (resonance with the C=O), giving the C–N bonds partial double-bond character, so they are shorter than a normal C–N single bond.

(i) σ: head-on (end-to-end) overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis.
π: sideways overlap of p orbitals, above and below the internuclear axis.

(ii) H–C≡C–H: 3 σ (two C–H, one C–C) and 2 π (in the triple bond).

Any one: all C–C bonds in benzene have equal length (and strength), intermediate between single and double bonds (bond order 1.5); the molecule is a regular hexagon. (Also: enthalpy of hydrogenation is less exothermic than expected.)

(i) • The H–X bonds are polar because of the electronegativity difference between H and the group 16 element.
• The molecules are bent (V-shaped) because of the two lone pairs, so the bond dipoles do not cancel – uneven distribution of charge.

(ii) From H2S to H2Te the number of electrons increases, so London (dispersion) forces increase and more energy is needed to separate the molecules. (H2O is anomalously high due to hydrogen bonding.)

NH2− has 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = 4 electron domains.

Electron domain geometry: tetrahedral
Molecular geometry: bent (V-shaped/angular), ≈105°

Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons).

(i) Structure I (O=C=O): O(1) = 0, O(2) = 0.
Structure II (O≡C–O): O(1) (triple bond, one lone pair) = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1; O(2) (single bond, three lone pairs) = 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.

(ii) Structure I – all formal charges are zero (minimal charge separation), so it is the preferred structure.

• O3 has bonds intermediate between single and double (bond order 1.5, delocalized), whereas O2 has a double bond (bond order 2), so the bond in O3 is weaker.
• A weaker bond needs less energy, so lower-frequency photons: O3 requires the longer wavelength.

• CO2 is a small, non-polar simple molecular substance with only weak London (dispersion) forces between molecules – little energy to separate them, so it is a gas.
• SiO2 is a giant covalent (network) structure – melting requires breaking many strong covalent Si–O bonds, so it is a solid.

Physical (any one): all C–C bonds have equal length/strength, intermediate between single and double (bond order 1.5); the ring is a regular hexagon.

Chemical (any one): benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition; it does not decolorize bromine water; only one 1,2-disubstituted isomer exists; its enthalpy of hydrogenation is less exothermic than predicted for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene (extra stability from delocalization).

(i) Structure I (octet): Br singly bonded to three O; Br has one lone pair; each O has three lone pairs; overall charge −1 shown with brackets. Structure II (expanded octet): Br with two Br=O double bonds and one Br–O− single bond plus one lone pair on Br.

(ii) Formal charge on Br = valence e− − nonbonding e− − ½ bonding e−. Structure I: 7 − 2 − 3 = +2; structure II: 7 − 2 − 5 = 0 (+1 if only one double bond). Structure II is preferred because its formal charges are closer to zero.

Geometry: trigonal pyramidal.

Reason: four electron domains around Br – three bonding domains and one lone pair.

Angle: ≈ 107° (less than 109.5° because the lone pair repels more than bonding pairs; accept 100–108°).

Any two: butanoic acid forms more/stronger hydrogen bonds (O–H…O, O more electronegative than N; can form dimers); it has stronger London (dispersion) forces (larger molecule, more electrons); it has stronger dipole–dipole forces (more polar). More energy is needed to separate its molecules, so it is a liquid.
The bond angles in a three-membered ring are about 60°, far smaller than the tetrahedral 109.5°, so the ring is highly strained (poor orbital overlap, weak bonds).

Any one: all C–C bond lengths are equal and intermediate between C–C and C=C (bond order 1.5); the ring is a regular hexagon with all angles 120°. (A Kekulé structure would have alternating short and long bonds.)

The π electrons are delocalized over O–C–O (resonance), so both C–O bonds are identical with bond order 1.5, intermediate between single and double.

Value: between C=O (122 pm) and C–O (143 pm) – e.g. ≈ 130 pm (123–142 pm accepted).

Two molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds between their COOH groups (C=O of one to O–H of the other, two H-bonds in a ring). In a non-polar solvent these are not disrupted by the solvent, so the pair behaves as one particle of Mr 244.
The O–O bonds in O3 have a lower bond enthalpy (weaker, longer) than O=O in O2: resonance/delocalization gives a bond order of 1.5 in ozone versus 2 in oxygen.

(i) N in the centre, single-bonded to two H and one Cl; one lone pair on N; three lone pairs on Cl.

(ii) sp3 (four electron domains).

(iii) Trigonal pyramidal; H–N–H ≈ 107° (100–109° accepted) – lone pair repels more than bonding pairs.

(iv) Coordinate (dative) covalent bond – the N lone pair is donated to H+.

(i) H–C≡C–H: each C shares three pairs with the other C and one pair with H; no lone pairs (H:C:::C:H).

(ii) The C≡C in ethyne is shorter than C–C in ethane because more electrons are shared (triple bond), giving a stronger attraction between the nuclei and the bonding electrons.

(iii) London (dispersion) forces – ethyne is non-polar. Just “intermolecular forces” or “van der Waals” is not accepted.

(i) The bonding is delocalized (resonance) – the π electrons are spread over the molecule; the real structure is a hybrid.

(ii) Linear – the central N has two electron domains (no lone pair), which repel to 180°.

(iii) sp.

O2: O=O double bond, each O with two lone pairs.

O3: O=O–O: central O has one double bond, one single bond and one lone pair; the terminal O atoms complete octets (double-bonded O has 2 lone pairs, single-bonded O has 3). The single bond may be shown as a coordinate bond (arrow). A single delocalized structure is not accepted here — draw one Lewis (resonance) form.

Reason: resonance — the π-bond electrons are delocalized over both O–O bonds, so the two bonds are identical (bond order 1.5).

Length: between the O=O (121 pm) and O–O (148 pm) values, e.g. ≈ 128 pm (any value 121 < length < 148 pm).

Any value 110°–119° (≈117°). Three electron domains around the central O give trigonal planar electron geometry (120°), but the lone pair repels more than bonding pairs, so the bent molecule's angle is slightly less than 120°.

SF4: S bonded to four F atoms with one lone pair on S (10 electrons, expanded octet); each F has three lone pairs. Five electron domains → see-saw geometry.

SCl2: S bonded to two Cl atoms with two lone pairs on S; each Cl has three lone pairs. Four electron domains → bent/V-shaped (≈ 103°, less than 109.5°).

Losing marks: forgetting the lone pairs on the F/Cl atoms.

SCl2 is more volatile than H2O (b.p. ≈ 59 °C vs 100 °C).

  • SCl2: polar bent molecule — dipole–dipole and London forces only (no H bonded to N/O/F).
  • H2O: hydrogen bonding between molecules, which is much stronger.
  • Although SCl2 has more electrons (stronger London forces), the hydrogen bonds in water need more energy to overcome, so water is less volatile.
Carbon I (CH3, four single bonds): sp3. Carbon II (part of C=C, three electron domains): sp2.

Sigma (σ): head-on (end-to-end, axial) overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis, e.g. s–s, s–p or p–p; electron density lies between the nuclei.

Pi (π): sideways (parallel) overlap of two p orbitals; electron density lies above and below the internuclear axis.

(i) σ: head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals, electron density concentrated along the line between the nuclei. π: sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals, electron density above and below the internuclear axis.

(ii) H–C≡N: 2 σ (C–H and one in C≡N) and 2 π.

(iii) sp (two electron domains, linear).

HCN is more polar (larger dipole, from the strongly polar C≡N), so it has stronger dipole–dipole attractions (some weak H-bonding) than HCl, even though HCl has a larger Mr and slightly stronger London forces.

O2N–NO2: an N–N single bond; each N forms one N=O double bond and one N–O single bond and has no lone pair. The double-bonded O has 2 lone pairs and the single-bonded O has 3 lone pairs. (Each N has a formal charge of +1 and each single-bonded O −1.)

(i) All N–O bonds are the same length (between N–O and N=O), so there is resonance: the π electrons are delocalized over each NO2 group (bond order 1.5).

(ii) About 120° (three electron domains around each N, trigonal planar; ≈117° accepted).
Both C1 and C2 (the C=C carbons) are sp2.

A double bond: one σ bond and one π bond.

  • σ bond: head-on (axial) overlap of an sp2 hybrid orbital from each carbon.
  • π bond: sideways overlap of the unhybridized p orbitals (one on each C).
  • The π electron density lies above and below the plane of the σ bond (prevents rotation).
